title: GPU Redistribution Burst Corridor Playbook
content:
PURPOSE
This playbook defines an operational procedure for initiating a fast, temporary redistribution of GPU capacity across regions (a 'burst corridor') to absorb sudden, multi-zone or region-level demand spikes and provide DR failover headroom. This is distinct from long-term warm-pool provisioning: corridor actions are intended to be fast, reversible, and minimize customer-visible latency regression.

SCOPE
- Applies to Hosted API and Dedicated clusters on public cloud regions only (private on-prem runbook TBD).
- Targets eviction-resistant workloads first (best-effort preemption for non-critical jobs).
- Focus: 1–12 hour elevated demand incidents or region degradation events where cross-region capacity transfer reduces risk.

BACKGROUND / RATIONALE
- Observed pattern: sudden model popularity surges plus regional infra incidents create transient capacity deficits. Spinning up new dedicated capacity takes time and may not be cost-effective for short events.
- The corridor approach temporarily increases egress routing and redistributes spare GPU inventory (elastic pools, preemptibles, burst buffer) across adjacent regions to maintain latency SLOs.

TRIGGER CONDITIONS (any one)
- Region P95 latency > 500ms sustained for 10 minutes AND sustained GPU utilization > 85% for 5 minutes,
- Route failure causing > 10% of requests to be retried or errored for 3 minutes,
- On-call or Incident Commander declares multi-zone outage with expected duration < 12 hours.

METRICS TO CHECK BEFORE ACTION
- Per-region GPU utilization (avg, p95) last 5 / 15 / 60 min
- Queue depth / queue wait time for token generation pipelines
- Active model shards and KV cache hotness distribution
- Cross-region bandwidth and estimated cost delta

ROLES & RESPONSIBILITIES
- Incident Commander (IC): declares corridor activation, approves cross-region routing changes.
- SRE Lead: executes routing policy changes, monitors infra health metrics.
- Capacity Engineering: decides which pools to drain/shift (elastic vs reserved).
- Network Engineer: validates egress and networking quotas (bandwidth, VPC peering).
- Customer Success on-call (optional): communicate to affected enterprise customers if SLA-impacting.

PRIORITY BURST CORRIDORS (ordering for selection)
1) Neighbor-region corridor: if region A suffers, route to adjacent region B in same geo (latency delta minimal).
2) Latency-tolerant pool corridor: route lower-priority / batch workloads to farther region C to free local GPUs.
3) Shared regional pool takeover: in emergencies, temporarily reassign Dedicated spare to Hosted tasks per contract rules.

STEP-BY-STEP RUNBOOK
1) IC verification (2–3 minutes)
   - Confirm trigger metrics.
   - Post brief summary to #incidents and ping SRE lead.
2) Rapid assessment (5 minutes)
   - Capacity Eng: list candidates for redistribution (elastic pools, preemptible lanes, non-SLA lanes).
   - Network: confirm cross-region bandwidth headroom and cost center approval for burst traffic.
3) Prepare routing changes (5–10 minutes)
   - Create policy: increase weight of Region-B endpoints by X% for affected model routes. Template: {model-route: greet-v2, shift: 30% -> region-b}. (Concrete weights below.)
   - Add TTL for policy: default 60 minutes; auto-revert after 2 hours unless extended.
4) Execute pool reassignments (5–15 minutes)
   - Drain selected nodes from local inference pools with graceful cutoff (drain-config: max-inflight=6, drain-timeout=120s).
   - Attach drained nodes to target corridor pool in Region-B as read-only cache with KV-prefix prewarm if available.
5) Monitor and iterate (ongoing)
   - Watch latency, error-rate, and cost-delta dashboards per 60s.
   - If downstream region B exceeds 90% utilization -> scale back corridor by 10–20% or activate next corridor.
6) Deactivation
   - When local utilization drops below 70% and p95 latencies are within SLO for 20 minutes, revert routing weights and reattach nodes back to origin region.
   - Run a sanity check for cache cold-start impacts and do a targeted prewarm if required.

WEIGHT GUIDELINES (example)
- Small event: shift 25% of best-effort routes to neighbor region.
- Medium event: shift 40–60% and thaw 10% of preemptible buffer.
- Severe/DR: shift up to 80% for critical models only, keep low-priority routes at 0%.

CAPACITY MATH EXAMPLE (quick sniff test)
- Region A demand spike requires +120 GPU-seconds/sec sustained.
- Region-B available spare capacity: 60 GPUs with 80% avg utilization => effective spare headroom = 60 * (1-0.8) = 12 GPUs.
- Preemptible lane recoverable: 40 GPUs, but 50% risk of eviction => conservative effective = 20 GPUs.
- Total immediate transferable = 32 GPUs. If each GPU supports 4 GPU-seconds/sec for target model, transferable throughput = 32 * 4 = 128 GPU-seconds/sec -> covers deficit.
- If not sufficient, escalate: request burst cloud allocation (cloud-burst ticket) or trigger customer-priority throttles.

SIMULATION & TEST NOTES
- Run tabletop every quarter with 3 scenarios: sudden traffic surge, inter-region peering outage, and cross-region cloud provider incident.
- Synthetic test: create controlled 30% request flood for a non-production model across one region and validate corridor activation / rollback timeline.

KNOWN RISKS & MITIGATIONS
- KV cache cold start: mitigation => prewarm top-10 prefixes and reduce burst shift for cache-hot models.
- Cross-region network cost: mitigation => limit corridor lifetime and route only high-leverage traffic.
- SLA contract violations for Dedicated customers: mitigation => preauthorize limited takeover amounts and require explicit IC signoff.

POST-INCIDENT CHECKLIST
- Confirm traffic returned to baseline for 30 minutes.
- Re-run consistency checks for model outputs across regions (sampling).
- Compute cost delta and annotate billing tags.
- Create incident writeup and add to confluence page.
- Action items: add any new warnings to the auto-triage rules.

OPEN QUESTIONS / TODOs
- Q: Should we support automated corridor activation based solely on metrics? (Pros: speed. Cons: risk of oscillation.)
- TODO: Add pre-approval templates for enterprise Dedicated contracts that allow specific takeover amounts. (Owner: Maya)
- TODO: Add a small on-call 'corridor budget' cloud spend approval flow to avoid manual exec signoff during nights. (Owner: Samir)

APPENDIX / QUICK LINKS
- Runbook ticket template: JIRA-ENG-1829
- Design doc: confluence://infra/burst-corridor-design
- Runtime PR for routing policy engine: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/458

NOTES TO SELF (informal)
- Keep corridor TTL conservative initially, increment after 3 successful drills.
- Consider implementing 'circuit-breaker' weight caps in the router to avoid cascading into farther regions.

END
